Knowns embedded text two ways: a local ONNX runtime linked into the binary,
and an OpenAI-compatible HTTP provider. The ONNX path carried a 35 MB
platform-specific shared library the release pipeline downloaded for five
platform/arch pairs, a loader probing five filesystem locations that had to
arch-match what it found, a model download command tree, and a tokenizer used
by nothing else.

This removes it. Ollama is also local — embedding still runs on the user's
machine and text never leaves it. What changes is the shape of the dependency:
from a library linked into the binary to a service the user installs and runs.

Two things had to hold first. Keyword search now survives an unreachable
embedder: hybridSearch computed keyword results and returned them alongside the
error, and Search discarded them. The ONNX path hid that, because a locally
loaded library is rarely unreachable. Once Ollama is the only path, "installed
but not running" becomes ordinary and the bug becomes the common failure.
Classification happens at the three embedder boundaries via an
errSemanticUnavailable sentinel, never by matching error text, so a
non-operational failure still errors instead of silently degrading.

the D2 default on every read, automatically. Writing is not automatic:
.knowns/config.json is committed, so a rewrite triggered by `knowns task list`
would put a change in someone's working tree they never made. `knowns migrate`
is the explicit path, versioned by a new config schemaVersion.

select one with `knowns config`. Projects on `provider: local` keep working and
should run `knowns migrate --write`; the migration marks the index stale rather
than reindexing, so search serves keyword results until an explicit reindex.

the well-sourced failures and the one convention that are the only real
knowledge the project memory holds. The sweep runs whenever the prompt
hook fires, so this was a working day or two from losing them.

The defect is the rule, not the number. Those entries accumulated under
a system that never surfaced the queue: nothing expired an entry and
nothing counted one, so a person could work here daily for months and
never learn that anything was waiting. The line that reports the backlog
shipped today. Retiring a proposal for missing a deadline that did not
exist is retroactive, and it takes real knowledge with it.

ProposalIsExpired now measures from the later of the entry's timestamp
and the day the rule took effect, so a backlog built in silence gets the
same full window as anything written afterwards. A fixed date rather than
persisted state: no migration, nothing to drift between machines, and
once the window passes it stops mattering and can be deleted.

Both expiry tests had to be rewritten. They anchored on time.Now and
happened to coincide with the effective date, so they proved nothing
about the rule they were named for; one of them also reached the sweep
only through CaptureWithOutcome and so could not choose a clock. They now
anchor on the effective date and drive the sweep directly.

feat(memory): inject memory claims, not whole memories

Injection showed exactly one memory per prompt, cut mid-sentence. Three
causes: serializeItems broke out of the loop on the first entry that did
not fit, discarding the smaller entries behind it; serializeItem trimmed
the body to whatever budget was left, and half a rule reads as a whole
one; and allowedCategory kept a second, drifted copy of the category
contract, so an active convention memory could top every search and never
reach an agent.

An entry is now emitted whole or not at all, carrying only its claim with
a pointer to the rest. On the real store a prompt injects four to five
memories intact inside the existing 2500-byte budget, where it injected
one truncated entry before.

The claim is split on RAW content: normalizeWhitespace collapses the blank
line separating a claim from its evidence, so anything downstream of it
has already lost the boundary.

fix(memory): fold diacritics in derived keys instead of shredding them

Replacing every non-ASCII rune with a separator destroys any language
written with diacritics: "Không dùng em dash trong nội dung" became
"kh-ng-d-ng-em-dash-trong-n-i-dung", which names nothing, cannot be typed
back from memory, and collides with any other title sharing those
consonants. Folding gives "khong-dung-em-dash-trong-noi-dung" instead.

The fold is NFD decomposition with combining marks dropped, plus an
explicit map for the letters that carry no combining form of their own.

feat(memory): let authors settle where a claim is cut

Injection shows only a memory's claim. Without a marker that boundary is
the first paragraph, which nobody chose and which a later edit to the
opening paragraph moves without anyone noticing.

memory add and update now report the claim they derived, its source, and
a warning only when the boundary is a guess. knowns memory migrate
previews the entries in that state and, with --write, inserts the marker
exactly where the split happens today.

Two things had to change for the migration to be behaviour-neutral, and
neither was obvious until it was measured against the real store.

The marker is a formatting directive, so it must be invisible to
anything that judges relevance. Indexing and tokenizing it made the first
migration run drop two memories out of a prompt's results entirely.
StripMemoryDetailMarker now runs before scoring and before chunking.

Inserting the marker must not touch UpdatedAt. That field feeds the
recency bonus, so a reformat was quietly raising every migrated entry's
score. UpdateContentPreservingTimestamp keeps it.

Verified by capturing the hook payload for three prompts before the
migration and after: byte-identical.

fix(memory): load user commitments at session start

The first injection of every session carried no user commitments. The
session-baseline tier existed and ranked correctly, but nothing reached
it, for three independent reasons.

A hook payload with no prompt field was returned whole as the prompt, so
a SessionStart envelope became the query. The baseline branch saw a
non-empty prompt and bowed out, and the session opened with whatever
shared a word with the hook's own JSON.

The baseline ranked by tags, a free-form field. Three of the user's four
preferences sat at positions 10 to 12 out of 12, below every project
failure note; the fourth led only because its author happened to tag it
"style". It now ranks by category, which the write path validates, with
tiers wide enough that tags and recency never cross them.

No SessionStart hook was installed. installClaude and installCodex both
deleted the group while runtime status still reported "installed". Both
now write it, and a half install reports "drifted" with the reason.

baselineMaxItems was also dead: its guard tested a field config always
fills. It is now a real ceiling.

fix(search): keep memory IDs through the SQLite vector store

Every global memory had lost the semantic layer, with no error anywhere.
The engine did search the global index and did find the right memory,
but the SQLite store persisted memory_layer and memory_store and never
memory_id, so the hit came back with an empty ID. The engine keys memory
results by that ID and the runtime hook drops any result without one.
The global index runs on SQLite, so this reached every global memory.

memory_id now round-trips the way decision_id already did. Rows written
before the column existed, including rows the legacy file importer
writes, are backfilled from the chunk id when the index opens. The
column stays the only place the ID is read from.

AddChunks and Search dropped DecisionID the same way, so decisions on
the SQLite backend lost their IDs too. Fixed on the same lines.

The hybrid path also required a shared word before it would consider a
semantic hit, which put keyword in front of semantic and discarded
exactly the matches the semantic layer exists to catch. The score floor
still applies.

Known consequence: global memories now reach hybrid scoring for the
first time, and that scoring was never calibrated for them. They can
displace a relevant project memory on an unrelated prompt until the
scoring is normalized.

fix(memory): judge relevance by cosine, not rank

Runtime memory injected unrelated memories and rejected precise short
prompts, for three measured reasons.

The hybrid boost was the engine's fused score, which is a rank:
reciprocal rank fusion divided by the best fused score, so the top result
is always 1.0. "ok cảm ơn" gave the em dash rule a full boost. The engine
now carries the best chunk's raw cosine as SemanticScore, and the hook
judges relevance on it against an absolute floor. On the live store,
prompts about a stored memory peak at 0.62 to 0.67; prompts about nothing
peak at 0.50.

Keyword overlap was a raw count times 0.35, so one memory scored 0.77 for
"em dash" and 2.52 for a longer paraphrase. It is now the share of the
prompt's content words, which a paraphrase does not change, and it only
breaks ties when the semantic layer ran.

The tokenizer only knew ASCII, so Vietnamese words with diacritics
shredded below the length filter while ASCII function words matched
everything. Tokens are now folded and function words dropped.

When the semantic layer found nothing relevant, the hook fell back to
keyword matching and injected anyway; that answer now stands. The sum
threshold for a lone item is gone, the floor applies before the item cap,
and a memory indexed in two stores is injected once.

The floor is calibrated for qwen3-embedding:0.6b and needs recalibrating
if the embedding model changes. knowns search --json gains semanticScore.
